1) here is the problem with labelling things as fake news (applies to all political identities). news is really 2 parts: fact + perspective
2) for the longest time newspapers were 99% perspective because facts had to be processed via words. then came cameras
3) even with cameras and then video which could capture facts, there were still only a few sources and they all packaged w/ perspective
4) now everyone has phone cameras and streaming, tweeting and blogging. facts and perspective have become unbundled
5) we've seen that ppl can have objectively different realities while living in the same place. experience same facts from diff perspective
6) not to mention that facts arent objective either, they are subject to biases of whoever "sampled" reality to record the fact
7) all of the sudden we are exposed to legitimately different facts and perspectives regarding the same time and place (and systems)
8) very few ppl know how to navigate this, but some have already figured out how to exploit it. we must adapt. we cant make news great again
@wblut my main point is that fact and perspective are constantly being conflated, out of confusion and for exploitation
@wblut also my point is that weve arrived here because of a collision between culture and technology.

4) I value community. Connecting with people who share my values. Working w/ them, eating w/ them, learning w/ them. understanding them.
5) I value building things. building to give people joy, building to help people work. Building because it makes me feel human.

Beyond excited to share the latest @distillpub article: Building Blocks of Interpretability
distill.pub/2018/building-…
An epic collaboration with @ch402 @arvindsatya1 @shancarter @ludwigschubert @hypotext and @zzznah introducing exciting techniques for looking deeper into ML models

The amazing @TwoMinutePapers released a great summary video of the article:
youtube.com/watch?v=pVgC-7…

You can also get a high level overview of the concepts from the @nytimes 
nytimes.com/2018/03/06/tec…

The article takes the Feature visualization technique from distill.pub/2017/feature-v… and uses it to turn "anonymous" activation vectors into "semantic dictionaries": a data structure where the keys are meaningful icons. This opens the door for very interesting interfaces...

Each of the hidden layers of the network can be thought of as a cube that can be sliced in different ways. Any of those ways can use Feature Visualization to create a foothold for a visual interface. So rather than trying to stare at array indices you look at little icons

@stamen <3 I can't take too much credit, this was really driven by @ch402 and @arvindsatya1 with transformative help from @shancarter @ludwigschubert @hypotext and @zzznah. I can say I learned an incredible amount working on it, I hope it does the same for others!
@storesyntax I'd probably use some d3, assuming you want to render with SVG. I'm currently loving vue.js for framework w/components and data binding and would use it to structure the app

For example you can visualize activations for each spatial position you get a sense of what the network is taking away from that part of the image. It's interesting to see a cross between a tennis ball and an apple in the dogs mouth (even tho its just dog lips in the photo)

Again, the feature visualizations give us something to look at, and once we have that we can start to investigate deeper, like showing how much particular spatial positions were activated. This helps us see what parts of the image were significant to the network at each layer

A fascinating technique we can add on is Attribution, previously people mostly looked at how the input image impacts the final classes, but we can actually see how spatial activations in one layer impact the next (or any other layer, including the output!)

learning #d3js is not learning how to make charts, it's learning how to turn data into graphics with web standards. the problem is one of perception and expectation setting. people say "I want to learn d3" but they really mean "I want to communicate complex data on the internet" x.com/Frankly_Data/s…

I think of web standards as the lowest common denominator for global communication. the graphics APIs are not ideal but if you want to instantly distribute your data-driven story to billions of people you can expect to pay the price of a small learning curve. x.com/Frankly_Data/s…

I don't think this is the trouble with d3, it's the trouble with people's dilluded expectations. this is like saying "the trouble with paintbrushes is to make a painting you must have a deep understanding of perspective, proportion, paint mixing and color theory" x.com/seecmb/status/…

to be fair, people see impressive and inspiring output, ask how it's made and people respond "d3". it's the tool that brings everything together, we just don't talk about the years we spent banging our heads against the browser, studying computer science, design, humanities etc

@Elijah_Meeks yeah, but I don't think the API surface is a big deal, it's a Swiss army knife and you can cherry pick. The gotcha is when people realize they need to learn all the other stuff below (browser/DOM/2D graphics) and above (design/color/data) when they expected simple magic

@jrm4 absolutely, I see the web as the lowest common denominator for humanity's computing needs. the abstractions available are a crazy mess which is part of why we need d3. a native scene graph with a good API would be great

@Elijah_Meeks yeah, but still I think it's a problem of perception not content. if someone knows a modern web framework they've learned a bunch of way weirder things already. virtual dom? lifecycle events? xhr is fundamental, d3.geo is for making maps that are too complex for leaflet.

@Elijah_Meeks instead of blaming d3 we should just change how we introduce it to people. Ive always said it's a utility belt, pick and choose what you need. it's all things that CAN be very handy while making data vis. reducing d3 footprint wont reduce the complexity of making/learning datavis

@Swizec @Elijah_Meeks but why should someone learn everything in d3? there are parts I haven't. I pick up what I need when I need it because I've internalized more fundamental aspects of web dev, 2D graphics, data analysis

the problem with the term actionable is that it seems to imply a presumed disengagement. "I only want to be bothered by this if it gives me something without any effort on my part."

on the surface it seems reasonable, we want to make things that have some kind of impact. the goal of most visualization is to communicate some understanding, and understanding could certainly lead to action.
One thing I wonder is how you are taking action currently? Are you literally blindly stumbling around? Wouldn't any sliver of light immeasurably improve your situation?

All libraries are just someone else trying to make a thing easier to do.

Frameworks are just someone's opinion on how to organize a handful of concepts and glue them together.

So what are these fundamentals?

I did nothing but #reactjs for a solid year in 2015. I didn't really touch it again until a month ago.

It felt like nothing changed in 5 years, because fundamentally nothing did.

This thread is not a personal response to the OP but an attempt to share my perspective with the community.

Anyway, the reality certainly is that there are a ton of ways to build things, and constantly adding more. It can be  hard to see where the fundamentals are underneath.

I remember when AJAX was the new hotness in 2005 (it had been in IE for 6 years at that point). IE6 still mattered. git was just invented. there were magazines about code.

Your struggle is real, here is a thread on why I think it's all gonna be ok. x.com/_lrlna/status/…

CPUs? yeah, at the end of the day you have one incredibly fast bean counter. Ok, maybe you have multiple cores, so you have a few bean counters. Fancy GPU? thousands of bean counters.

Still, your program is asking one bean counter to count a bunch of beans as fast as it can...

I don't mean for you to learn the whole TCP/IP stack, but a solid understanding of how data goes from one computer to another goes a really long way. The client-server paradigm, browser sandbox rules, fuckin CORS... knowing this well can unblock so much.

After scope comes the concept of asynchronous. This one's a bitch. Your program is no longer a straight line. What's in or out of scope is essential AND hard to see directly.

async is also where knowing about 2 lower level abstractions is really helpful: networking and CPUs...

Then comes JavaScript. The core of all programming is variables, functions and loops. Cool, the hard part is scope. Especially in JS. Get that shit down so that when you are reading code you know exactly what is in and out of scope.

The core is HTML. It's rules are simple until you add on CSS and start thinking about layouts.

Understanding the ways to layout DOM elements (without frameworks, preprocessors etc.) is key #1 to not getting overwhelmed by new shit.

not even talking styles, just layout.

At the end of the day we are all just trying to get the web browser (a program with a bunch of fancy APIs) to execute in a particular way when a user accesses our URL.

Those APIs can do a lot of cool things, but the core hasn't really changed since 1999.

Also if all you have are existing patterns it's easy to get stuck in a situation where none of your patterns fit. It can be tempting to start pulling patterns off the shelves (there are so many!)

But I believe that contributes to the exhaustion folks feel.

I think another big factor in the explosion of web libraries and frameworks is all the "patterns" they are providing.

Personally I struggle to understand the value of a pattern until I run into a problem where the pattern fits, usually after I've tried my own inelegant hacks.

There are many fancy tools for this, but console.log and a return statement is all you absolutely need.

Fundamentally you want to be able to tell if some unexpected behavior is coming from 1) the environment 2) the libraries 3) your code
(it can actually be any combo as well...)

it's everyone who wrote a library you are depending on, and everyone they depended on, and so on.

If you can isolate EXACTLY what is being asked and by whom you can get to the bottom of any bug.

I believe this is a skill that can be actively developed.

Alright, so having solid fundamentals in what you're asking the network to do and what you're asking the CPU to do gives you solid footing.

The next skill is what let's you ignore 99% of the JavaScript ecosystem: isolation.

It's not just you asking the CPU for a favor...

There are two ways to make code go faster: 1) ask your bean counter to count fewer things or 2) figure out how to divvy up your beans among different bean counters, just make sure you and they don't get confused about which beans go where.

To be honest, I love it. I hope more people make more libraries. 

Once you have the fundamentals and a little taste it's pretty easy to benefit from a nice idea and ignore all the noise.

I bet that last sentence applies to any human creative endeavor...
♥️

I think developing a taste for patterns comes from experience and deliberate practice.

You may notice that when you get the chance to apply a pattern to a problem it can be quite satisfying. You may rush to create an npm package so others can benefit. And that's how we got here.

Knowing the fundamentals means you can make your own patterns tailored to the situation you find yourself in. You don't HAVE to... god knows I use a ton of libraries. But you also don't HAVE to keep up with the latest thing, you can afford to wait for the good ones to win out.

The #d3js community is huge, it's grown in so many places from so many disciplines over the years. To properly celebrate we need your help!

Shirley (@sxywu) and Seemant have put together this form to gather as many perspectives as we can:

docs.google.com/forms/d/1Nn0Gm…

I'm excited to share a big event for #d3js, celebrating 10 years of open source data visualization!

we're putting together a meetup on Feb 17th, RSVP:
meetup.com/D3-Online/even…

we want to celebrate the history and growth of our community as well as look to @d3js_org's future!

The D3 Community Leads will be formally introduced, a group of folks pretty much anyone reading these tweets will recognize as major contributors to the community.

These folks are coming together to reinforce the strengths of our community and guide more explicit improvements!

I'm really excited about the agenda, I'll do a tweet per agenda item:

* Introducing the D3 Community Leads by Ian Johnson
* Timeline of D3 History by Christophe Viau
* Words from Mike Bostock
* Announcing the D3 History Parade with Shirley Wu & Seemant Kulleen
* Q&A Session

A fun fact about the kick-off event is that it is exactly 10 years to the day from the first public release of #d3js:
github.com/d3/d3/releases…

thanks to @kerryrodden for pointing out the 1.0.0 release date last year so we could properly prepare 🎉

A Timeline of D3 History will be presented by none other than @d3visualization who has been cataloging the community and its wonderful & varied contributions since pretty much the beginning.

He's been pulling together various data sources to visualize 10 years of visualization!

We will also announce something I'm incredibly excited about, a D3 Parade!

What is that you ask? Well, Shirley (@sxywu) and Seemant will be telling you all about it on the 17th. It's something you'll be able to participate in and I expect it to be both fun and rewarding 😁

Of course there wouldn't be #d3js without @mbostock or such a welcoming and humble community without his leadership. A lot of lessons have been learned in the last 10 years, and Mike's vision for the future of D3 and data visualization are sure to inspire ❤️❤️❤️ & 🧠🧠🧠

Finally, we will close out the event with Q&A for the speakers. We have a huge and passionate community and I'm sure there will be many questions. 

We'll make sure there is a way to submit questions before hand as well so folks have a chance to think about them.

so here's to 10 years of #d3js and looking forward to another 10 years of amazing data visualizations! 🎉🎉🎉

I have shunned MATLAB for Python, I have sipped vintage FORTRAN 77 and published Java Applets at the turn of the millennium. I want to offer a grounded perspective on the benefits of doing science online.

As a Master's student in a newly formed Department of Scientific Computing I learned from applied mathematicians, physicists, materials scientists, biologists, geologists, statisticians and engineers. My program was a survey of computational methods and how to apply them.

I was quickly drawn to the discipline of scientific communication, entranced by the papers, talks and posters that were able to convey new and fascinating concepts to me as well as frustrated by those that... didn't.

I also learned that scientists use many different environments, often incompatible with and even incomprehensible to each other. Demonstrating a result was one thing, getting someone else to repeat that result on their machine was entirely another.

The reasons for any given scientist using any given environment were often great, it was where the existing toolset for the discipline was, it was where the compute was. But if you wanted to use an idea that came from somewhere else, well, good luck.

As computing infra has improved and standardized, the various scientific communities have come closer together.  the state of the art in large scale computation has become much more cosmopolitan.

The state of scientific communication is still firmly in the grips of the PDF.

The web was born of the desire to share scientific knowledge, yet has remained a frontier for scientific communication for decades. It is often seen as the lowest common denominator of programming environments, and for this very reason it is also the most accessible.

to get the total weekly passenger throughput we can use temporal binning to get this familiar line chart and sum up all the airports together.

with Plot a quick swap of Plot.lineY with Plot.rectY lets us see how the daily throughput of each airport adds up to the total

ive been reflecting on my career and two topics have been bouncing around in my head recently:

🧠💼knowledge work
💻🌳computational environments

i think the two make up 80% of the skills required for successful data analysts, data scientists, data engineers and data visualizers

whether your running a jupyter notebook locally, spark job on a cluster or observable notebook in the browser you will run into a limit of your environment.

really understanding the underlying 💻🌳will allow you to move data and processing to where it is best suited

all of the data professions require an understanding of where data lives, how big it is, how long it takes to process in different ways, how to move it around and transform it. they care to different extents and different levels of detail.

eventually all hit a speed limit: 💻🌳

the 💻🌳 is the first principles of programming, you cannot not know the answers and expect to build anything.

you can know the minimum and build toys, learn some things, but the limits of your abilities will always be set by your understanding of the 💻🌳

first lets talk computational environments 💻🌳

where does the code you write run? where does the data it reads and write live? what kind of connections does it have to other computers?

the answers to these questions are fundamental, unavoidable yet so often glossed over

all of the data professions are ultimately about gaining understanding of systems that can be shared with others, i.e. generating knowledge 

the fundamental skills all share the same base of computation with different specialization in techniques.

both can be taught better

to me "no code" is the promise that a company will supply a computational environment 💻🌳 akin to Disney Land. 

they will dictate every aspect of the computational experience from how long your requests wait in line to what kinds of data you can use.

maybe that's perfect!

we want our code to run all the time, or at a specific time, or respond within a reasonable amount of time, or to handle many requests at once and to tell us when something goes wrong and to backup in case it does and...
all of these expectations are handled (or not) by the 💻🌳

i like the term "just code" here because it captures a common and reasonable sentiment, that i want to just code.

i disagree with "accidental complexity" tho, it is no accident, it is the accumulation of expectations of the computational environment 💻🌳 x.com/paulbiggar/sta…

it's pretty reasonable to base an entire career on really knowing one 💻🌳, which usually means a programming language + local dev setup + community packages + some kind of deployment

but if you understand 💻🌳from first principles you can move between worlds and build quickly

another important aspect of 💻🌳is the libraries of code available. this is often discussed in relation to the programming language but really it's what's "installed" on the machine running your code.

most of what we do is adding a thin layer of logic on top of existing packages

in data science you build models of data to enable prediction and classification of new data.
explaining the capabilities and limitations of the models is just as important as keeping them updated and upgraded with your peers

in data analysis you go through a process of hypothesis generation and investigation, leading to insights about the domain you're working in.
explaining the insight to your clients is just as important as verifying the methodology with your peers

in data engineering you build systems that take in data from various sources and supply data to other people and processes for further use. it's equally important that the output is understood by your clients and the process is understood by your peers

ive done data engineering, data analysis, data science and data visualization in different combinations for the last 10 years.

getting people to understand what i'm doing (including getting myself to) is the core challenge, a skill i'm thinking of as 🧠💼

what i'm trying to get across is that your computational environment 💻🌳 is always there, and wether you choose to shape it or not, it shapes your code.

now let's see how the same applies to knowledge work 🧠💼

but likely you will hit some limit that the no code environment doesnt account for or is unwilling to support and you'll need to setup your own environment.

depending on the size of the project it could be a weekend with open source or an entire multidisciplinary team effort
observable notebooks create a 💻🌳 in the browser that allows for faster 🧠💼 especially for data visualization and increasingly for data analysis

github started as a 🧠💼 tool for software developers to share process understanding. it didnt take long for a lot of 💻🌳 tools to get attached to it (github actions!)

jupyter notebooks is a mix of 💻🌳 with 🧠💼 because it enables sharing a (piece) of the environment

something i'm realizing about both 🧠💼 and 💻🌳 is that the skills are often confused with the tools that enable them, and that different disciplines have more or less tooling to support aspects.

lets look at a few examples

so that makes me think there are two main branches of knowledge work 🧠💼

1. sharing the results of your understanding
2. sharing the process of your understanding 

both are fundamental to any data career and both are learnable skills

in each of the four disciplines i'm pointing out the direct output along with the future looking considerations of either maintenance or verification. maybe youre a team of 1 so your peers are your future selves.

in data visualization you represent data in visual forms that enable us to leverage our eyes to recognize patterns our words can't capture.
its equally important that the visualizations are consumable by your clients as they are maintainable by our peers

thinking of a tool as a space that people enter helps me see it from different perspectives.

lots of possibilities can be exciting! or overwhelming, or even limiting.

remember the age old saying:
if you have a hammer🔨 everything looks like a nail💅

tools 🛠 create a possibility space, they enable a new set of abilities, often a combinatorial explosion.

skills 🧭 are the paths you take in the possibility space. highly skilled people move quickly and seem to teleport to interesting possibilities

so how does that help us?

something i've been thinking about is the difference between tools and skills

especially from the perspective of working on tools for professionals

when should you build more features vs spend more time teaching?

a useful framing recently came to mind:

recognizing that the tool creates possibilities leads me to a helpful principle for designing tools especially with the constant pull to make things "simple" or "easy to use"

don't kill possibilities. dont cut off potential paths.

its not ease of use, its about not feeling lost

if you can find your own way through the possibility space of a tool 🛠 to do something useful, you have acquired a skill 🧭

no doubt some simply have a better sense of direction, or those early adopters have a stronger sense of adventure. but everyone must navigate these spaces

lets be more specific than learning. the person wants to navigate this space to get to the possibility they can see because of the tool.

how do we navigate? we plan our route with maps 🗺 we follow trails left by others📍we hire a guide or we stumble around feeling our way thru

so depending on where someone is coming from the same explosion of possibilities can feel very different!

presumably the person has arrived because they want at least one of those possibilities realized. they want a path to that ability.

thus they must "learn"

so we want to familiarize people with the possibility space, help it feel less foreign even if its a wildly new technology.

my biggest inspiration currently is national parks. nature provided the possibilities and we visit, taking different paths 🧭

and when it comes to teaching skills, its not so much about showing possibilities (features) its about helping people navigate.

that could mean better signage (in product help), better maps (docs), billboards (examples), guided tours (courses) or playgrounds (tutorials)

i finally figured out why i hate the term "actionable insight" so much after chatting w/ @mrejfox recently.

as in "this dashboard needs to surface actionable insights"

it's because there are at least 4 steps to go from insight to action. its a process not a product. the steps:

step 2: ask a follow up question.

in 100% of cases a single insight will not be enough to drive an action. context will need to be gathered, comparisons made, questions asked.

this is challenge #2 with designing data vis, details on demand.

lets say questions were answered...

step 1: noticing a pattern. this is what an "insight" is, a pattern that is either unexpected or meaningful in some way.

this is challenge #1 with designing data vis, the meaning comes from the data & its context.

but lets say you succeed in surfacing a meaningful pattern...

step 4: take action

yay! our insight was made actionable! we got a promotion! 

lol. 

in retrospect the insight was obvious. everyone thoroughly understands the current reality. no one remembers holding wrong beliefs. can't you make this dashboard more actionable?

step 3: make a decision

this is an important distinction because often multiple people are involved in making a decision, and they can be different from those taking the action.

a decision needs support, context and often leads to a plan of action...

Introducing Latent Scope: a new open source instrument for visualizing unstructured data

The process has 6 steps:
1. Ingest: load in a CSV or Parquet file, or use the python interface to load in a pandas dataframe
2. Embed: choose from ~20 embedding models
3. UMAP: play with the parameters that work for your data
4. Cluster: run HDBSCAN and tweak the params
5. Label:…

Latent Scope is not just embeddings though, it's actually two pieces: A python-driven data process and a Javascript-driven visualization interface.

pip install latentscope

The process helps you experiment with generating embeddings, UMAPs and clusters. The web interface helps…

The point of the process is to get to the exploration interface.

When you're exploring a dataset, you can pan, hover and select as well as peruse your clusters and take a closer look at the patterns found in the embeddings.

The easiest way to manage the process is through the web interface, which takes you step by step.

The web interface just calls the python scripts tho, so if you wanted to do anything piecewise or automate some parts in your own pipeline that's easy too!

Back in 2016 I was working at Google and had the immense fortune to co-author some articles for the newly formed Distill publication
distill.pub

while working on these articles I learned about several incredibly powerful concepts...

here is my talk from the @mozillabuilders demo day! a quick 8 minute introduction to Latent Scope, what it is and how I came to build it.

I'm also posting each slide in this 🧵

follow along for a quick journey into latent space 🗺️

and what's more high dimensional than the internal representations of machine learning models?

it turns out models find patterns in data, and surfacing those patterns gives you a whole new perspective on data
distill.pub/2016/handwriti…

the first of these concepts is dimensionality reduction.

you may be familiar with t-SNE, or the more modern and efficient UMAP algorithms

if not, they take data points that are similar in high-dimensions and place them close together in 2D
distill.pub/2016/misread-t…

this really became clear to me when I got involved with open sourcing half a billion QuickDraw sketches and then supporting the SketchRNN project

hand-drawn sketches are the definition of unstructured data, but SketchRNN could find structure in them
medium.com/@enjalot/machi…

one way to surface those patterns is to map out the hidden states using dimensionality reduction techniques

when you UMAP the activations, you get different areas representing different concepts the model has learned
distill.pub/2019/activatio…

when you map out the hidden states from SketchRNN activated on drawings of faces

in one corner of the map, you have sketches of not-quite-smiling faces...

realizing this potential to find patterns lead me to apply these techniques to production data.

I lead a project inside Google Cloud to map out user behaviors of millions of cloud users across hundreds of products.

in another corner of the map you have people who are really good at sketching!

i couldn't formulate a query that would give me this batch of images, but the model recognizes them as similar, and my eyes do too

but then i left stability and found myself GPU poor.
I worried I'd hit my own personal scaling wall...

but a funny thing happened

later, I worked at stability.ai and applied the same techniques to curate millions of high signal training images from user generations

we could even see what kinds of images were being generated each day

people were using them in production RAG systems
yet blissfully unaware of how their data actually looks 👀

so in the beginning of 2024 I set out to build Latent Scope. I wanted an easy way to explore unstructured data that anyone could use locally.
github.com/enjalot/latent…

I looked around and realized that you didn't need huge infrastructure or clusters of H100s to be working with tons of embeddings on production data!

there were all kinds of high quality open embedding models that you could even run quickly on a CPU

One of the challenges with 3D is plotting too many points at once. Sure we can render many points but once they are all on top of each other can you make sense of them? One fun experiment is to do a "voxel heatmap" where we bin the points in 3D and interact with a slice

I've been using Moonshine a lot for work, which means theres been a ton of iteration on it. It's transformed into an article writing harness, helping me surgically remove slop from my technical communications. 🔪

Let's look at what the harness does!

Another thing thats a pain to prompt but easy to do yourself is re-arrange blocks of text or figures. Everything in a moonshine article is draggable in edit mode, just hold cmd and drag the block!

A big motivation is to avoid dropping into a code editor or back to prompting

For an interactive article we need interactive figures. Agents are damn good at making these now, but often we want to fiddle with the parameters. Rather than re-prompt for every small tweak, the agent can easily setup knobs you can interact with and save directly to the article

Moonshine is a skill that builds a small React project focused on turning markdown into interactive explanations. It's got a number of interesting features now that offer direct manipulation of the output.
Let's start with editing prose inline with a cmd+click

One of my favorite things has been using comments to pepper a freshly generated article with specific feedback on blocks and figures then letting the agent go. Moonshine has a file based protocol for managing the comments that makes it reliable.

can't talk about direct manipulation without a nod to @worrydream! Moonshine supports tangled words out of the box. Have links drive interaction in figures, don't force people to imagine the link between what their reading and what they can click on!

In a similar vein, generated diagrams are easy to make but hard to perfect. Moonshine uses React Flow and stores the positions of the nodes and viewport for you. Arrange things exactly how you want the reader to see them. Direct manipulation ftw!
